L169@P4: He was involved in a very interesting joint book project with top young Brazilian mathematician Leopoldo Nachbin who, just 6 years older than Grothendieck, had reached sudden
L170@P4: and international fame at age 22 with a paper establishing a bound on the growth rates
L171@P4: of an analytic function. Those who knew Nachbin perceived him as being dynamic and
L172@P4: highly energetic; always on the go, travelling frequently between France, the US and Brazil,
L173@P4: writing many dozens of letters to his mathematical friends and sending postcards (often
L174@P4: depicting charming girls) to the others, as well as participating in the role of editor in an
L175@P4: astonishing number of journals and book series for which he tirelessly recruited articles.
L176@P4: But Dieudonn´e expressed serious doubts that the joint book would ever get off the ground,
L177@P4: because Nachbin was “Brazilian, and so inclined to indolence”, as he said forthrightly,
L178@P4: though not unkindly. Certainly Dieudonn´e cannot easily have found a match to his own
L179@P4: brand of unflagging devotion to even the most thankless parts of mathematical work anywhere, but he still found Nachbin’s lightheartedness exaggerated: “Schwartz remembers
L180@P4: that in 1952, after promising to write up his lectures, he didn’t even produce 3 pages! Now,
L181@P4: you’re over there, so you’re the best judge of Nachbin’s degree of enthusiasm, but I think
L182@P4: it’s only right to warn you.” By December 1954, the plan of the book was complete, with
L183@P4: the first part intended to introduce the classical theory that Grothendieck had explained
L184@P4: in his two-year course, based on the copious and detailed notes for that course that had
L185@P4: been typed and bound by the University of S˜ao Paulo (with an introductory chapter by
L186@P4: Barros Neto), and the second meant to cover the theory of tensor products and nuclear
L187@P4: spaces, the whole not to exceed 600 pages. Perhaps the project was too similar to work
L188@P4: that Grothendieck had already written up extensively, or perhaps Nachbin’s enthusiasm
L189@P4: waned; in any case, Dieudonn´e was perfectly right, and no book was ever produced∗.
L190@P4: From all these observations, it would appear that although Grothendieck did profound
L191@P4: work in his first year in S˜ao Paulo, he did not undergo another flash of discovery of the

L194@P4: every Banach space possesses the “approximation property”. A space X is said to have this
